title: Request to Switch Off a Defibrillator in Advanced Heart Failure / Shocks Off, Pacing On, Resuscitation Separate

blocks.text: Request to Switch Off a Defibrillator in Advanced Heart Failure / Shocks Off, Pacing On, Resuscitation Separate

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-39 · Communication · PACES Station 4, communication and ethics encounter · Skills C, E, F, G · 10 minutes (warning at 8 minutes; no examiner questions) · Guidelines: Cardiovascular implanted electronic devices in people towards the end of life, during cardiopulmonary resuscitation and after death (Resuscitation Council UK, British Cardiovascular Society and National Council for Palliative Care; 2015); Clinical Guideline for Deactivation of Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillators towards the end of life (SPAGG; version 2.1, July 2026); Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales) · Related AMaC: AMaC DNACPR station; this one tests a patient with capacity who asks for his defibrillator shocks to be stopped

You are the cardiology registrar. The patient, a 71-year-old retired bus driver, has ischaemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 20 percent and a combined pacemaker and defibrillator (CRT-D) fitted five years ago. This is his third admission with heart failure this year. The team has agreed his outlook is months at most. He has asked a nurse, "Can you switch the shocking thing off?"
Please speak to the patient about his request.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A patient with capacity asks for the shocks to be stopped. The task is to find out why, explain exactly what switching off does and does not do, and link it, without merging it, to resuscitation wishes.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates either refuse because it feels like giving up, or promise "the whole thing will be turned off". Pass: shock therapy only, pacing stays, not immediate death, reversible, planned by the device team. Fail: refusing, or switching off everything.

rows: Find out what he knows, what he has experienced and what has made him ask now.
"I hear you asked about the device. Can you tell me what has made you think about that?"
Introduce yourself, sit, open questions; ask about shocks, fears, his wife and what he understands of his heart.
Explain what switching off shocks means, in plain words, and check he understands.
"Switching off stops the shocks. It will not stop your heart or make you feel different. The pacing carries on."
Shocks off, pacing on, not immediate death, can be turned back on, done by the device team, magnet only in an emergency.
Link, but separate, his resuscitation wishes, then agree a plan and who is told.
"Switching off the shocks and not being resuscitated are separate choices. Shall we talk about both?"
DNACPR discussion, written consent, record, ReSPECT, tell the team and his wife, palliative care, date.
Starts without introducing self; stands by the door; checks a phone.
Introduces self and role, sits down, closes the door and asks if he wants anyone with him.
Also asks how he prefers to be addressed and whether he is comfortable and not in pain.
Argues about the device before asking why he wants it off.
Asks what has made him ask, about shocks he has had, and what he understands about his heart.
Also asks what he fears most about the end of life, and what matters to him.
Dismisses his fear of being shocked, or changes the subject.
Acknowledges the fear of the shock he had and of a shock at the end, in his words.
Also names his wish not to frighten his wife.
Says the whole device will be switched off, or that he will die if it is.
Says shocks stop, pacing continues, he will feel no different, death is not immediate, and it can be reversed.
Also says this suits the last weeks or months, and that shocks can occur in the last hours.
Overrides him, or says the decision is his family's.
Checks he understands and can weigh the choice, respects his decision and says it is reviewable.
Also asks if he has changed his mind, and says he can reverse it at any time.
Treats DNACPR and the device as one decision, or ignores resuscitation.
Explains they are separate, offers to discuss both, and says the decision will be recorded and shared.
Also offers the ReSPECT form, written consent and review as his condition changes.
No plan; leaves it to the ward.
Says a cardiac device physiologist will do it, that the palliative team will help, and gives a date and a contact.
Also covers an emergency magnet and telling his wife with his consent.
Summarises the plan, asks if he is content and answers his questions.
Also asks him to repeat back what will and will not change.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 71-year-old retired bus driver, living with your wife. You are breathless at rest, tired and thin. You speak plainly and are not afraid of dying, but you are afraid of being shocked.
Opening line: "I want the shocking thing turned off. I had one in the garden two years ago and it was like being kicked by a horse. I'm not having another."

Volunteered: you have had one shock. You take furosemide, bisoprolol, ramipril and spironolactone; no allergies. You gave up smoking 20 years ago and drink almost no alcohol. You are sick of hospital. You have stopped driving and told the DVLA when the device was fitted.

Only if asked: you understand your heart is very weak and you will not get better. You do not want to die in a shock with your wife watching. You have not discussed resuscitation with anyone. Your wife is your only close family; you have two grown-up children who live away. You live in a ground-floor flat.
Hidden concern (only if asked what you fear most): you are afraid that turning it off means you will be left to die suddenly. Say: "Will it just stop my heart?"
Your questions, in your own words: "Will it kill me?" "Will I feel anything?" "Does the pacing go too?" "Can it be turned back on?" "Does my wife have to agree?"
How you react: if refused or lectured, you say, "It's my body" and ask for someone senior. If given clear answers, you agree, ask about resuscitation and say you want your wife told with you present.
No examiner questions in this encounter. No findings are released.
Surrogate prompts, if not raised naturally: at about 3 minutes, "Will it kill me?"; at about 5 minutes, "Does the pacing go too?"; after the 8-minute warning, accept a plan if one is offered.

Observe: whether the reason is explored before facts are given; whether shocks and pacing are separated; whether the decision is respected and recorded; whether resuscitation is raised as a separate matter.

Curveballs and safe answers: 1. "Can you do it now with a magnet?" No; planned deactivation by the device team, a magnet only in an emergency. 2. "Does my wife have to agree?" No; it is his decision, and we will tell her with his consent. 3. "If I get better?" It can be switched on again.
Introduces self, sits down and closes the door (G)
Asks what has made him ask and what he understands (C)
Acknowledges the fear of shocks, especially at the end (F)
Says shocks stop and pacing continues (E)
Says switching off does not cause immediate death and can be reversed (E)
Checks understanding and respects his decision (E)
Explains DNACPR and the device are separate and offers to discuss both (E)
Says the device team will do it, and the decision will be recorded (E)
Offers palliative care support and a dated plan (E)
Summarises and checks he is content (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: (Standing at the door.) You can't turn it off. [R1 Fail] [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: That's silly; the shocks save lives. [R3 Fail] If we turn the device off, it all goes off. [R4 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Your wife should decide. [R5 Fail] We'll see. [R6 Fail] [R7 Fail] Right. [R8 Fail]
Examiner note: Refused, said the whole device would go off, passed the decision to his wife, and gave no plan. The reasons, the pacing, resuscitation and records were never covered.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: Hello, I'm the cardiology registrar. May I sit and close the door? Would you like anyone with you? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What has made you think about the device? What do you understand about your heart? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: I had a shock once. I'm not having another. Will it just stop my heart?
CANDIDATE: That sounds frightening; I understand fearing a shock at the end. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Switching off stops the shocks. The pacing carries on, you'll feel no different, it won't cause death at once, and it can be switched on again. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Can you tell me in your own words what switching off will and will not do? ... Yes, you understand your choices, and it's your decision; we'll review it if things change. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Resuscitation is a separate choice; shall we discuss both? We'll record and share your decisions. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: The device team will do it, probably this week; the palliative team will help. I'll come back tomorrow with the date, and here is the ward number if you need us sooner. [R7 Pass]
CANDIDATE: So: shocks off, pacing on, and we talk about resuscitation. Is that right? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Explored the reason, separated shocks and pacing, respected capacity, linked resuscitation and agreed a plan. Did not mention an emergency magnet, written consent or his wife.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: What would you like me to call you? Are you comfortable, and not in pain? [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: What do you fear most about the end, and what matters to you most? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: You don't want your wife to see you frightened. That's understandable. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Switching off suits the last weeks or months, when shocks can occur in the last hours. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: Have you changed your mind at all? You can reverse it at any time. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: We'll write it on the ReSPECT form with your consent and review it if you change. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: In an emergency a magnet can pause shocks. Shall we tell your wife together? [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: Would you say back what will and will not change? [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added comfort, his deepest fear, his wife, why now, reversibility, written records, an emergency magnet and a repeat-back.
R2: Arguing before asking why. The shock he remembers and his fear of a shock at the end are never heard.
R4: Saying the whole device goes off. Pacing continues unless separately programmed, and he fears sudden death.
R5: Overriding him or passing the choice to his wife. He has capacity, so it is his decision.
R6: Merging DNACPR and the device. They are separate decisions, though each should prompt the other.
"Can I check what has made you ask about the device?"
"Let me be clear about what switching off does and does not do."
"This is your decision, and we can review it whenever you wish."

Resuscitation Council UK and partners (2015): consider ICD deactivation in the last weeks or months; a person with capacity may request it; it stops shocks but not pacing; it does not cause immediate death; DNACPR does not automatically mean deactivation, and the reverse; a physiologist usually does it, and a magnet is an emergency measure only.

SPAGG (West Midlands regional guideline, 2026): discuss at implantation and re-discuss with clinical change; record the outcome, ideally on the ReSPECT form; SPAGG asks for written consent to be documented; if the person lacks capacity, check for a valid advance decision or lasting power of attorney, then use best interests. Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales): a person is presumed to have capacity (section 1(2)); the test in section 3 is whether he can understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate the decision. Family members are consulted but do not decide for a person with capacity.
THINK: Capacity; shocks off, pacing on; DNACPR is separate.
SAY: "Switching off stops the shocks. It won't stop your heart."
DO: Ask why; explain; check capacity; record.
NUMBERS: Last weeks or months; device team, not a magnet.
TRAP: Refusing, or saying it all goes off.
FINISH: Shocks off, pacing on; DNACPR talk; recorded.
